Question: The number of distinct points in the \(xy\)-plane common to the graphs of \[ (x+y-5)(2x-3y+5)=0 \] and \[ (x-y+1)(3x+2y-12)=0 \] is:
Solution:
A product of real numbers is zero exactly when at least one factor is zero. Thus we can interpret each graph as two lines without expanding the products. The first graph consists of
\[
x+y=5,\qquad 2x-3y=-5,
\]
and the second consists of
\[
x-y=-1,\qquad 3x+2y=12.
\]
A common point must lie on a line from each graph, but different pairs might give the same intersection.

Start with \(x+y=5\) and \(x-y=-1\). Adding the equations eliminates \(y\), giving \(2x=4\). Hence \(x=2\) and \(y=5-2=3\). This point also satisfies the other two line equations, since
\[
2(2)-3(3)=-5,\qquad 3(2)+2(3)=12.
\]
Therefore all four lines pass through \(P=(2,3)\).

Their slopes, in the order listed, are
\[
-1,\quad \frac23,\quad 1,\quad -\frac32.
\]
These slopes are different, so the four lines are distinct. Two distinct lines cannot share a second point, because two distinct points determine exactly one line. Consequently, every pair formed by choosing one line from each graph meets only at \(P\).

This includes every possible common point and counts the repeated intersection only once. The number of distinct common points is therefore \(\boxed{1}\), choice \(\boxed{\text{B}}\).
